prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map captures an outdoor paved court bordered by a grassy strip and a dense tree line about 10–15 m behind a basketball hoop pole, followed by an open court with a low building roughly 30–50 m away in frames 4–5. As the camera wearer approaches the hoop from about 4–5 m away in frame 1 to directly underneath the rim (within 0.5–1 m vertical reach above the head) in frames 3–4, an airborne basketball in front of the pole in frame 1 (around 3.5–4 m away, just below the backboard) disappears before the wearer turns around in frame 5 to face a man standing roughly 3–4 m ahead to the left of center, with nothing within arm's reach in frames 1, 2, and 5. In frame 5, the man faces and looks toward the camera wearer with his lower legs and feet slightly clipped by the bottom frame edge, while in frames 3–4 the hoop rim and net are partly cropped on the right edge above the wearer. The map clearly separates the foreground hoop, mid-air ball, pole, and approaching man from the distant trees and sky—even where strong sun glare washes out the backboard in RGB—and shows a continuous ground-plane distance gradient. However, the depth map is unreliable inside the transparent backboard and through the open mesh of the net in frames 2–4, where it assigns a flat foreground depth across the empty holes rather than the background sky depth.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates only a few foreground regions against a black background across the outdoor basketball court, failing to segment the court, trees, or the airborne basketball in frame 1 (about 3.5–4 m in front of the camera wearer) and leaving everything out of arm's reach except the overhead rim in frames 3–4. As the camera wearer moves from 4–5 m in front of the hoop (frame 1) to 2–3 m away (frame 2) and then directly beneath the rim looking up (frames 3–4, within 0.5–1 m reach), the map segments the rectangular backboard in frame 2 (excluding the net blocking its lower center) and the circular rim/net on the right side of frame 3, plus a diagonal building roofline on the lower left of frame 4 about 30 m away. In frame 5, after the wearer turns 180 degrees away from the hoop, the map segments the man standing 3–4 m in front and slightly left of center—who faces and looks toward the wearer with his ankles occluded by the bottom image border—as well as a tiny distant person silhouette roughly 25–30 m behind his right shoulder. While this map highlights the tiny background person in frame 5 that is nearly invisible in the RGB strip and cleanly outlines the man's silhouette, it is highly unreliable in semantic classification and recall. Specifically, it mislabels the backboard as a 'tv' in frame 2, the close-up basketball rim/net as a 'clock' in frame 3, and the distant school roofline as a 'train' in frame 4, while completely missing the hoop in frames 1 and 4.
descriptions.pose: The body and hand pose map renders only yellow body skeletons on a black background—with no magenta hand skeletons detected in any frame—across the sequence where the camera wearer approaches the basketball hoop (frames 1–4) and turns around toward the open court (frame 5). In frames 2, 3, and 4, when the wearer is 2–3 m in front of the pole and then directly underneath the overhead hoop (within 0.5–1 m vertical reach), no skeletons are present because no people are in the upward-tilted field of view. In frame 5, the map accurately places a frontal yellow torso-and-limb skeleton on the man standing 3–4 m in front of the camera wearer and slightly left of center, showing his shoulders square to the camera, his head facing toward the wearer, his arms hanging at his sides with nothing in reach, and his feet near the bottom frame boundary. What the pose map reveals—and where it is simultaneously highly unreliable—is a false-positive yellow human skeleton in frame 1 at the center of the image (about 4–5 m away), where the detector mistakes the round orange basketball (just below the backboard) for a head/raised arm and the vertical hoop pole beneath it for a narrow torso and legs facing sideways. Furthermore, the map fails to detect the distant people standing 25–30 m behind the main person in frame 5 and provides no fine-grained hand keypoints.
